prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, whose magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms brought optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as a single prize. After round 1 the case is stronger on the points I care most about, not because more members name it but because the objections raised against it were about category and not about the science. The achievement is specific: the magic-wavelength condition lets one trap thousands of neutral atoms with the light shift cancelled on the clock transition, which removes the old trade-off between confinement and perturbation and gives ensemble statistics. Ye's group then showed that this scheme reaches fractional uncertainty near 1e-18, and the many-body and spin-polarised-fermion work explained why high density is an asset and not a liability. Independent Sr, Yb and Hg clocks and direct inter-laboratory comparisons confirm it, and it has already delivered centimetre-scale gravitational redshift measurements and tighter bounds on drifting constants. The two-name credit maps onto the concept and first strontium demonstration (Katori) and the record accuracy and many-body physics (Ye). The 2005 comb prize solved counting optical cycles and the 2012 prize concerned control of single quantum systems; neither credited ensemble interrogation in a magic-wavelength lattice, so I do not see double recognition. The chair asks whether the clock needs a partner part. I think not: the committee has honoured single coherent achievements with two names before, and attaching a second field mostly adds an attribution problem.
statement.case_against: The serious objection, pressed by Mehlig, Olsson and Johansson, is that this is a superb refinement of the frequency-standard programme and that no deviation from existing theory has been seen, so the prize rewards an instrument and not a discovery. I cannot refute that on a definition of discovery; I can only say that Alfred Nobel's text allows discovery or invention and that a change of several orders of magnitude in what is measurable is a change in physics, because it opens questions that could not be asked before. Attribution is the second weak point: Lemonde, Pfau, the Paris and Braunschweig groups and the wider Boulder environment contributed, and a two-name prize will look narrow to part of the community. Third, the redefinition of the second has not happened, which a sceptic can use to argue for waiting. Finally, Kroll rightly notes that two atomic physicists agreeing is not independent evidence, and I have tried to test my view against the objections of colleagues outside my field.

responses.point: The clock is a refinement of the programme honoured in 2005 and 2012, and no new physics has yet been seen, whereas the Z2 classification introduced a new principle.
responses.response: I accept that B008 introduced a principle and that the clock is not that kind of achievement. But the question what physics the clock has taught us has partial answers already: it resolves gravitational redshift over centimetres, it has tightened bounds on variation of constants and it created a controlled many-body system with measured interaction shifts that fed back into clock design. A null result at 1e-18 is itself information. On B008 I agree with Mehlig that the quantum spin Hall pairing of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is natural and that the 2016 prize did not cover time-reversal-invariant insulators, but the unresolved credit to Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and to Fu, Kane and Mele versus Moore and Balents keeps it, for me, below the clock on attribution.

responses.point: Twisted bilayer graphene is a discovery that opened a new regime, whereas the clock is an invention and its main consequence has not occurred.
responses.response: I keep B029 as my first alternative and agree it opened a new platform. Our difference remains maturity. If the citation names only the flat-band prediction and the correlated insulating and superconducting states, the settled core is real, but the superconducting mechanism and the device-to-device twist-angle variation are open, and Cao, Fatemi and Dean complicate the experimental credit; I think the committee should not take that risk and also overlook the cleaner case. I take her point that the redefinition of the second is pending, but I do not accept that it measures the prize: the clocks are already compared at 1e-18 between laboratories, and the redefinition will follow from that, not precede it. I note and welcome her statement that she would not object to the clock winning.

responses.point: The clock should be paired with a discovery-type achievement, IceCube credited to Halzen alone, because it may not suffice by itself.
responses.response: I take the chair's pairing seriously, and I agree that IceCube's diffuse flux is a secure discovery. But my answer to his question is that the second part should not be added merely to give the clock a discovery partner. I cannot identify a decisive individual contribution that separates Halzen from Karle and Yoshida in a collaboration of hundreds that grew out of AMANDA, and a one-name credit beside a two-name credit would look arbitrary to the community. If the committee insists on two parts, I would rather accept B010 only with an attribution that the members who know the field, Pearce and Danielsson, can defend jointly, and within the three-person cap that would force a drop of one of Katori or Ye, which I will not support. I therefore prefer the clock alone.

responses.point: B043 is more an advance in measurement than a conceptual breakthrough, and measurement prizes should be tied to demonstrated fundamental results.
responses.response: I agree the citation should rest on demonstrated results, and I propose wording that names the magic-wavelength lattice and the 1e-18 performance and not the redefinition of the second. Danielsson's own view that the lattice idea is distinct from the comb and that the confirmation in Sr, Yb and Hg is unusually strong is the core of my case. Where we differ is the second part. I share his conclusion that IceCube without a clean credit is a weak half; he said he would rather drop it than invent a trio, and I think that is the better judgement, which leaves the clock alone as the coherent outcome.

responses.point: Agreement between two atomic physicists is not independent evidence, and the test is whether a non-specialist can see what changed; also the credit should not be widened to comb-era names.
responses.response: That is a fair challenge. The non-specialist test is satisfied by the centimetre-scale gravitational redshift measurement and the inter-laboratory comparison, which one does not need atomic theory to appreciate. I agree on not widening credit to the comb era, since that would blur the distinct lattice step. I would add one qualification to his framing: I would not rest the citation only on metrology, because the many-body clock results are physics results and the citation should signal that.

responses.point: Circuit QED is a different achievement from the 2025 macroscopic quantum tunnelling prize and does not duplicate it.
responses.response: I accept that distinction: the 2025 citation concerned tunnelling and energy quantisation in a Josephson circuit, while circuit QED concerns light-matter coupling and readout. My timing worry is therefore not logical overlap but the optics and practical consequence of a second superconducting-circuit prize within two years, together with the four-name credit that cannot be cut to three without dropping Blais or Girvin. Given his own conflict disclosure and his naming of B043 as the first alternative, I read his position as compatible with the clock being the consensus outcome.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat an instrument-level breakthrough as a discovery or invention within the intent of the prize; this is the main disagreement and not resolved by evidence.
Whether two names fairly represent a field in which Lemonde, Pfau, the Paris and Braunschweig groups and the wider Boulder group also contributed.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be read as evidence of impact or as a reason to wait; I judge it as the former.
Whether my own judgement of B029, B008 and IceCube, which lie outside my field, rests on too general a standard.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. From my profile: long-running collaboration with Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, papers with Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, and training in Ingvar Lindgren's Gothenburg group. None of these is a documented connection to Katori, Ye or their groups, and I have no connection to Halzen, Karle or Yoshida, so no specific conflict is apparent for B043 or B010. Kroll's note that he spent time in Hall's laboratory and Olsson's note on Japanese ties are for the chair to judge; they do not alter my own assessment. As an atomic physicist my views on B043, B006 and B027 may be tied to my field, and I have tried to test them against colleagues outside it. I changed nothing in my preferred configuration; the citation wording is sharpened to name the magic-wavelength lattice.
